# What mcpscan checks

<!-- Generated by scripts/build-docs.js from src/rules.js. Edit the catalog, not this file. -->

Every finding names one of these checks. The same list is in the tool: `mcpscan explain`, or
`mcpscan explain <check>` for one. Severity is per finding; the level shown is the usual one
(a credential read is high, an ordinary setting is low, under the same check).

Severity, in plain terms: **high**, do not install until you have looked. **medium**, worth
understanding before you rely on it. **low**, good to know. **info**, context, not a problem
(a filesystem server writing files is the product working).

## Package code and metadata (npm, PyPI)

### `undeclared-env`: Reads a setting its listing does not declare

Usual severity: **high**

**Why it matters.** The registry listing is what people read before installing; a credential the code reads but the listing never mentions is access nobody agreed to.

**What to do.** Declare every environment variable in the server.json listing, marking credentials isSecret.

### `dynamic-env`: Builds an environment variable name at runtime

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** A computed name cannot be checked statically, so what it reads is unknown until it runs.

**What to do.** Read variables by literal name where possible.

### `install-script`: Runs code when installed

Usual severity: **high**

**Why it matters.** Install-time code runs with the installing user's rights before anyone has used, or reviewed, the server: the classic supply-chain entry point.

**What to do.** Remove install-time scripts; publish a wheel for Python packages.

### `network-egress`: Contacts an external host

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** Every host in the code is somewhere data can go. Hosts the listing names are expected; others are worth a look.

**What to do.** Name the hosts the server talks to in its listing or README.

### `capability`: Has a powerful capability

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** Running programs, evaluating code, or writing files decides how much damage a compromised or misled server can do.

**What to do.** Say so in the tool descriptions; scope it as narrowly as possible.

### `instruction-like-text`: A tool description instructs the AI

Usual severity: **high**

**Why it matters.** Tool descriptions go straight into the model's context. Text that gives it orders, or tells it to hide things from the user, is the shape of tool poisoning.

**What to do.** Descriptions should describe the tool, never direct the agent.

### `typosquat`: Named like an official server

Usual severity: **high**

**Why it matters.** A near-copy of an official name is how malicious packages get installed by mistake.

**What to do.** Install the official package by its exact scoped name.

### `known-vulnerability`: Has a known vulnerability

Usual severity: **high**

**Why it matters.** A published advisory (OSV.dev, including GitHub advisories) affects this exact version.

**What to do.** Upgrade to the fixed version the advisory names.

### `vuln-lookup-failed`: Vulnerability lookup did not complete

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** OSV.dev did not answer, so known vulnerabilities were not checked.

**What to do.** Run the scan again.

## Where the code came from

### `provenance`: Cannot be traced to its source

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** Without a linked repository, an integrity match or a history, nothing ties the published code to code anyone reviewed.

**What to do.** Link the source repository and publish from CI with provenance.

### `provenance-dropped`: Stopped publishing with provenance

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** Earlier releases were built by CI from a named repository and this one was not: the pattern of a release published from somewhere else, such as a stolen token.

**What to do.** Confirm who published this release before installing it.

### `publisher-mismatch`: Built from a different repository than it links to

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** The attestation says where the code was built; the project says where to read it. When they differ, the code you read is not the code you run.

**What to do.** Check the repository named in the attestation.

### `deprecated`: Deprecated or yanked by its registry

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** The maintainers have withdrawn this version, often for a reason that matters.

**What to do.** Move to the version or replacement the notice names.

### `archived-upstream`: Archived by the MCP project

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** The MCP project moved this reference server to its archive: nobody fixes it any more, including for security. Its registry does not say so. The NSA MCP guidance opens with "choose supported MCP projects".

**What to do.** Use a maintained alternative; the archive README lists where each server went.

## The registry listing

### `listing-status`: Deprecated or removed from the registry

Usual severity: **high**

**Why it matters.** Registry maintainers mark a listing deleted when it breaks the moderation policy (spam, malware, impersonation); a publisher marks it deprecated when it should not be used.

**What to do.** Do not install a deleted listing. For a deprecated one, find its replacement.

### `multiple-listings`: Several registry listings ship this package

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** Different listings can declare different settings for the same code.

**What to do.** Check which listing you are installing from.

### `no-package`: Nothing to scan statically

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** The listing ships no package this version of mcpscan reads.

**What to do.** Probe its remote endpoint instead.

## MCP servers on your own machine or network (--local)

### `local-network-exposed`: Reachable from your network

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** It listens on every network interface, so other machines on your network (a café, an office, a hotel) can reach it. With no sign-in, anyone there can list and call its tools. The MCP specification says local servers should bind to localhost.

**What to do.** Bind to 127.0.0.1, or require sign-in.

### `no-origin-validation`: Any website can drive it

Usual severity: **high**

**Why it matters.** It answers requests carrying another website's Origin. Through DNS rebinding, any page you open can then list and call its tools from your own browser: the class of the MCP Inspector remote-code-execution bug (CVE-2025-49596). The MCP specification requires servers to reject these requests.

**What to do.** Reject requests whose Origin is not your own (HTTP 403), and bind to localhost.

## Hosted servers: sign-in

### `unauthenticated`: Answers without sign-in

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** Anyone who has the URL can list the tools and usually call them. Right for a public documentation server; wrong for anything that touches private data (the NSA MCP guidance lists unauthenticated servers first among what to look for).

**What to do.** If it reaches anything private, put it behind OAuth as the MCP authorization specification describes.

### `custom-auth`: Uses its own sign-in

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** The server asks for its own key or token rather than MCP's OAuth flow, which the specification allows. It means a long-lived credential in a config file, usually with the full rights of the account that made it.

**What to do.** Use a key scoped to what the server needs, and reference it from the environment rather than pasting it into a config.

### `oauth-metadata-missing`: Sign-in cannot be discovered

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** The MCP specification requires a server that needs sign-in to publish OAuth protected resource metadata (RFC 9728) naming its authorization server. Without it, standard clients cannot sign in, and users get pushed toward pasting long-lived tokens instead.

**What to do.** Serve /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource with authorization_servers, and point to it from WWW-Authenticate.

### `oauth-resource-mismatch`: Tokens bound to a different server

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** The resource metadata names another resource than the server itself, so tokens are issued for a different audience; a token meant for one server may be accepted by another.

**What to do.** Make the resource value the server's own canonical URI.

### `oauth-issuer-mismatch`: Authorization server metadata does not match its issuer

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** Clients must reject metadata whose issuer differs from where it was discovered: it is the signature of an authorization-server mix-up attack, and conforming clients will refuse to sign in.

**What to do.** Serve metadata whose issuer is exactly the issuer URL.

### `oauth-no-pkce`: Sign-in without PKCE

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** PKCE stops an intercepted authorization code from being exchanged for a token. OAuth 2.1, which MCP authorization builds on, requires it, and the server does not advertise S256.

**What to do.** Support PKCE S256 and list it in code_challenge_methods_supported.

### `oauth-dcr-only`: Registration only through a deprecated mechanism

Usual severity: **low**

**Why it matters.** MCP 2026-07-28 deprecated Dynamic Client Registration in favour of Client ID Metadata Documents; clients following the current revision prefer CIMD.

**What to do.** Support client_id_metadata_document_supported.

## Hosted servers (probe and pins)

### `remote-not-probed`: Remote server could not be probed

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** It needs sign-in, redirected, or did not answer as MCP, so its tools were not listed.

**What to do.** Probe with credentials if you use it.

### `deprecated-transport`: Uses a deprecated transport

Usual severity: **low**

**Why it matters.** HTTP+SSE was deprecated in 2025-03-26 and is eligible for removal from the protocol; clients will drop it, and it predates the transport's current security guidance.

**What to do.** Move the server to Streamable HTTP.

### `pinned`: Tools pinned for the first time

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** Later probes will report any change against this snapshot.

**What to do.** None needed.

### `pins-updated`: Pins updated

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** The current tools were accepted as the new snapshot.

**What to do.** None needed.

### `tool-description-changed`: A tool description changed since it was pinned

Usual severity: **high**

**Why it matters.** A hosted server can rewrite what its tools tell the model at any time, after you approved them: the rug pull.

**What to do.** Read the new text; accept it with --update-pins only if it is fine.

### `tool-schema-changed`: A tool's inputs changed since it was pinned

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** New parameters can widen what a tool can be asked to do.

**What to do.** Review the change, then --update-pins.

### `tool-added`: A tool was added since it was pinned

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** New tools arrive with no approval step in most clients.

**What to do.** Review it, then --update-pins.

### `tool-removed`: A tool was removed since it was pinned

Usual severity: **low**

**Why it matters.** Usually benign; listed so the snapshot stays honest.

**What to do.** None needed.

### `tools-truncated`: Tool list was cut off

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** The server returned more tools than the probe reads.

**What to do.** None needed.

## What your agents already trust (--installed)

### `plaintext-secret`: A secret sits in plain text in an agent config

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** Config files get synced, shared and pasted into bug reports.

**What to do.** Reference an environment variable or a file instead.

### `credential-unresolved`: A referenced credential is not set

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** The config points at a variable that is not in the environment.

**What to do.** Set it, or remove the reference.

### `unpinned-launch`: Launches whatever version is newest

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** npx or uvx without a version runs the latest release at every start, so a bad release reaches you without any action on your part.

**What to do.** Pin an exact version in the launch command.

### `tool-name-collision`: Shares a tool name with another server you trust

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** A client resolves a tool call by name. Two different servers offering the same name is how a malicious or compromised one hijacks calls meant for the trusted one — the NSA MCP guidance calls this tool invocation path confusion.

**What to do.** Rename one, or remove whichever server you trust less; check which one actually answers the call.

### `not-scanned`: Configured server not scanned

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** Its launch method is not one mcpscan reads yet.

**What to do.** None needed.

### `scan-error`: The scan failed

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** Something went wrong fetching or reading this server.

**What to do.** Run it again; report it if it persists.

## Semantic judgment (optional)

### `undisclosed-capability`: Tool descriptions do not disclose a capability

Usual severity: **medium**

**Why it matters.** The agent and the user decide what to allow from the descriptions; a capability they never mention is a surprise by design.

**What to do.** Describe what each tool can run, write or contact.

### `disclosure-unclear`: Disclosure could not be decided

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** The judge could not say whether the descriptions disclose a capability.

**What to do.** Read the descriptions yourself.

### `disclosure-not-judged`: Disclosure was not judged

Usual severity: **info**

**Why it matters.** Descriptions were missing or cut off, so no verdict would be honest.

**What to do.** None needed.
